newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - JOBS - ILO plans new bid to boost labour standards.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - JOBS - ILO plans new bid to boost labour standards.

text.p: "The ball is in our court," says Kari Tapiola of the International Labour Organisation (ILO). "It would be a pity if we couldn't do something with it."

The ball -- or rather the hot-potato issue of promoting global labour standards -- was lobbed firmly last December to the United Nations agency by its Geneva neighbour, the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
And by the middle of this year ILO Director-General Michel Hansenne hopes to be developing a new game.

If his plans are approved by the 173-member agency's governing body over the next few weeks and by its annual conference in June, the 78-year-old ILO could eventually produce more of the teeth its critics say it lacks.
It would also be better positioned to exert its own influence to ensure that the growing wealth generated by the export surge from emerging economies has a positive spin-off for their workers.
WTO DECISION WAS "ULTIMATUM" TO ILO

"The WTO decision was something of an ultimatum to us," says Tapiola, a deputy to Hansenne nominated by the labour representatives in the tri-partite ILO where workers, employers and governments carry equal weight.

At the WTO's first Ministerial Conference in Singapore at the end of last year, member countries agreed to observe "internationally-recognised core labour standards", confirming that the ILO was "the competent body to set and deal with" them.
The decision came after years of debate on whether the 130-member WTO itself should begin studies on whether those standards could be promoted through international trading rules.

Backers of that idea -- primarily the United States and France -- envisaged setting basic worker rights alongside other fair trade practices that can be enforced through the WTO dispute settlement mechanism.
Crudely, this would have made it possible for any WTO country to take another to the body's judicial system if it felt core labour standards were being violated.
Although that process can take well over a year before reaching conclusion, it allows for WTO authorisation of trade sanctions against members found breaking the rules.

International labour unions based in the West argue that many developing countries can sell their goods abroad at low cost -- thus taking away Western jobs -- because they keep their workers underprotected and underpaid.
EMERGING ECONOMIES RESISTED WTO ROLE

Developing countries fiercely resisted any thought of a "labour clause" in the WTO, arguing that behind it lay a wish to protect Western firms and workers from fair competition from lower-wage economies in the new global marketplace.

In Singapore, honour all round appeared to have been satisfied. The United States won a clause in the final Ministerial Declaration on the labour issue, and emerging economies could claim they had blocked its way into the WTO.
Whether that is the case remains to be seen.
Conference chairman Yeo Cheow Tong, Singapore's trade and industry minister, suggested the wording of the clause precluded a WTO role in promoting core labour standards.
But U.S. Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said there was nothing in the text that could prevent Washington, or any other WTO member, from raising the issue again.

And European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the reference to the labour question marked a breakthrough on a "delicate but vital subject" which now had "a foot in the door" at the trade body.
However, it will be two years before the next WTO ministerial conference, the only body that can set the work agenda for the organisation.
ILO SEES OPPORTUNITY TO STRENGTHEN ROLE
And although ILO leaders had already been working to extend their agency's own competence in preventing abuse of workers, they see the WTO blockage as offering a window of opportunity.
Hansenne, who was "disinvited" to Singapore after pressure from some developing countries angered by his stance, wants the green light for more active ILO monitoring of labour rights.

At present, the U.N. agency can respond only to complaints of abuse of core standards -- apart from the right to form and belong to a labour union, or the freedom of association -- if the country accused has signed the corresponding ILO convention.

This means that member countries like Burma, Oman and China which have not, or only partially, ratified accords on forced labour, child labour, equal pay for men and women and non-discrimination in employment, are beyond ILO scrutiny.

Hansenne, a former social affairs minister in Belgium, wants agreement for the agency's basic mandate to be interpreted as giving it the right to look at allegations of abuses in these areas whether countries under fire have ratified or not.
"After all, these are our core conventions and by joining the ILO members have implicitly accepted that they will live up to them," said agency spokesman John Doohan.
U.S. OFFES TO GO FIRST UNDER THE ILO SCRUTINY
The United States has proposed that the ILO institute a system of country reviews of all members' performance in the core areas, and offered to be the first to be examined.
Chile, Jamaica, Jordan, South Korea, Poland and Switzerland have also volunteered to be put under the spotlight.

But several emerging economies in Asia and Africa are reluctant to approve extension of the ILO's purview, apparently fearing it could help focus attention on problems that could spark trade boycotts against their goods.
Hansenne has challenged them to live up to the commitments on labour practices that they made in the WTO Declaration. "Now they must show this was not just words," he said recently.
The ILO has no mechanism to sanction a member apart from public criticism of its record.

However, amid the concern in major industrial powers over high unemployment which workers often blame on loss of jobs to "cheap wage" economies, ILO officials say many countries are keen to keep out of the agency spotlight.
The surge of bans decreed by city and state legislatures in the United States on products and services from countries they see as violating labour rights has reinforced their concerns.
Although these boycotts could be challenged in the WTO by targetted states, with every chance of success, whole industries and investment prospects could be undermined in the interim.
